text:
Supreme Court of Newfoundland and Labrador,
Court of Appeal

Lasade Enterprises Ltd. v. Newfoundland

Date: 1993-11-08

Graham Watton, Q.C., for the Appellant;

Bruce Piller, for the Respondent.

(1992 No. 215)

November 8, 1993.

[
1
]

Cameron, J.A.
:
This is
an appeal and cross-appeal of a decision of a board of arbitrators appointed
pursuant to the
Expropriation Act
,

R.S.N. 1970, c. 121 (now
R.S.N. 1990, c. E-19). Numerous grounds of appeal were cited by the parties.
Many of these overlap. The primary issues are:

(1) Whether the board
erred in either using or failing to make use of certain hearsay evidence;

(2) Whether the board
should have, in valuing the appellant’s land, considered the “freeze” on
development of the lands imposed by the Municipal Plan;

(3) Did the board err
in arriving at the market value by incorrectly applying the principles of
valuation.

Background

[
2
]

The appellant (Lasade) was one of several owners
who had lands at Corner Brook expropriated for the purpose of construction of a
bypass on the Trans Canada Highway. Other lands owned by Lasade were
injuriously affected. For the purpose of this case, it does not matter whether
the land was injuriously affected or expropriated as the parties agreed that
the parcels which were injuriously affected by expropriation would be valued as
if they had been expropriated and Lasade would convey those lands to the Crown
for the value determined by the board. Whether expropriated or injuriously
affected, the lands will be referred to as the “expropriated lands”. The parties
also agreed that the date of valuation was the date of expropriation, July 2,
1991. The expropriated lands were vacant at the time of expropriation.

[
3
]

A board of arbitrators was established to
determine the compensation to be paid to all of the owners in the locality. The
valuation of the Lasade lands was the first task undertaken. There were seven
parcels valued. These were identified as Parcels A, 1, 2, 5, 6, 9 and 10. All
of these lands are located in the same general area, though they do not all adjoin
each other. Both parties disagree with the decision of the majority which
awarded compensation to Lasade of $543,720, the appellant arguing that this
amount is too low and the respondent that it is too high. The minority report
determined compensation should be $1,342,010.80 and it is this amount which the
appellant seeks in compensation. All references to the decision of the board
are, of course, to the decision of the majority.

The
Role Of The Court Of Appeal

[
4
]

It is clear that this court will not interfere
with the award of a board of arbitrators unless it has proceeded upon a wrong
principle of law or has misdirected itself with regard to some material fact
resulting in an award of compensation which is clearly excessive or wholly
inadequate (
Miller et al. v. Newfoundland
(1977), 14 Nfld. &
P.E.I.R. 110
;
33 A.P.R. 110
;
13 L.C.R. 322 (Nfld. C.A.)
;
Associated Builders
Ltd. v. Minister of Public Works
(1978), 19 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 371
;
50
A.P.R. 371 (Nfld. C.A.)
;
Atlantic Shopping Centres Ltd. v. St. John’s (City)

(1985),
1985 CanLII 1876 (NL CA)
, 56 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 44; 168 A.P.R; 44 (Nfld. C.A.)).

Hearsay

[
5
]

Lasade takes the position that the board was in
error in rejecting the hearsay evidence of Marc Andrews, an expert witness,
regarding the motivation of persons who sold certain of the expropriated lands
to Lasade. However, it also argues that the evidence of Patrick Ryan, who was
not declared to be an expert, regarding an offer of sale of a comparable
property to Newfoundland and Labrador Housing Corporation was inadmissible and
should not have been used by the board because the evidence amounted to
hearsay.

[
6
]

Evidence of a statement made to a witness by a
person who is not himself called as a witness is hearsay and inadmissible when
the object of the evidence is to establish the truth of what was contained in
the statement (
R. v. O’Brien
,

1977 CanLII 168 (SCC)
, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 591; 16 N.R. 271).
There are numerous exceptions to this rule. These exceptions are founded on
necessity and circumstances which would support the trustworthiness of the
statements. One such exception is the one afforded to experts who are called to
give opinion evidence. It has long been accepted that in the course of forming
their opinions experts may refer to and rely on texts, research, works in their
field of expertise or discussions with others learned in the same field. This
is considered to be an “acceptable hearsay component in the makeup of every
expert’s knowledge which is drawn upon in formulating the opinion” (
The Law
of Evidence in Canada
by Sopinka, Lederman and Bryant, p. 547).

[
7
]

There is, however, another type of hearsay
evidence used by experts in forming their opinions: facts specific to the case,
not within the personal knowledge of the expert but gained by the expert from
another source. There was a time when the opinion of an expert, based on such
hearsay, could only be accepted if the facts, as opposed to the body of
professional knowledge, were then proven through other evidence, not hearsay.
This is clearly too strict a view at this time.

[
8
]

Psychiatrists regularly rely on medical
histories. In the field of real estate appraisal, it is common for appraisers
to use data respecting comparable sales which may be acquired from others. The
expert’s hearsay evidence of this type is admissible. It would clearly
complicate and unduly prolong hearings to require direct evidence respecting
each sale used by the appraiser to form his or her opinion.

[
9
]

In
R. v. Lavallee
,

1990 CanLII 95 (SCC)
, [1990] 1 S.C.R.
852; 108 N.R. 321; 67 Man.R.(2d) 1; 55 C.C.C.(3d) 97; 76 C.R.(3d) 329; [1990] 4
W.W.R. 1, the court considered just this issue, albeit in the context of a
criminal trial. Wilson, J., for the majority, acknowledged that the opinion of
an expert based in part on hearsay is admissible but added the proviso that
where the factual basis for the expert’s opinion is a melange of admissible and
inadmissible evidence the duty of the trial judge is to caution the jury that
the weight attributable to the expert testimony is directly related to the
amount and quality of admissible evidence on which it relies. However, the
words of Sopinka, J., in a concurring decision are instructive. On pp. 899-900
[S.C.R.], he indicates that in respect of the hearsay evidence obtained by the
expert within the scope of his expertise:

“The expert arrives at an opinion on the
basis of forms of enquiry and practice that are accepted means of decisions
within that expertise. … For a court to accord no weight to, or to exclude,
this sort of professional judgment, arrived at in accordance with sound …
practices, would be to ignore the strong circumstantial guarantees of
trustworthiness that surrounds it …

“Where, however, the information upon
which an expert forms his or her opinion comes from the mouth of a party to the
litigation, or from any other source that is inherently suspect, a court ought
to require independent proof of that information. The lack of such proof will,
consistent with
Abbey,
have a direct effect on the weight to be given to
the opinion, perhaps to the vanishing point.”

[
10
]

In
Saint John (City) v. Irving Oil
Co.,

1966 CanLII 64 (SCC)
, [1966] S.C.R. 581; 58 D.L.R.(2d) 404, the court held that the opinion of an
appraiser based on unrecorded interviews with 47 persons was admissible. The
frailties of the evidence were relevant only in assessing the weight to be
attached to the opinion.

[
11
]

An example of hearsay which should be afforded
little if any weight may be found in the evidence of a number of the experts in
this case who indicated the position of the municipality regarding rezoning or
services by reference to the opinion of an unnamed person in a particular
department. Under such circumstances, it is impossible for the other party to
perform an independent check on the statement in contrast, say, to data from
the Registry of Deeds which is readily available to anyone. Further, evidence
which comes from an interested party is suspect and should be proven in the
normal way though it must of course be recounted by the expert as a basis of
his or her opinion.

[
12
]

In this case, one of the experts, Marc Andrews,
gave hearsay evidence respecting the motivations of those who had sold the
expropriated lands to Lasade or its shareholder. On the basis of this
information, Mr. Andrews decided to ignore the purchase price to Lasade when
forming an opinion respecting the market value of these same lands on
expropriation. This hearsay “motivation” evidence is also one of the bases upon
which Lasade attacks the opinion of Gordon Brewer, an expert called by the
respondent, who utilized the purchase price to Lasade in forming his opinion.

[
13
]

The board, in arriving at its own opinion of
market value, did not assign substantial weight to motivational factors. While
the evidence was very important, it did not have circumstantial
trustworthiness. In spite of a directive of the board that it be done, Lasade
had not given the respondent a copy of the experts reports prior to the hearing
thereby depriving the respondents of the opportunity of independently checking
the information; and, there is nothing to indicate that direct evidence on the
subject was not available. For these reasons, I find no fault with the board’s
decision to give no “significant weight” to the hearsay evidence respecting
motivation nor with its conclusion that this type of evidence required direct
evidence.

[
14
]

Lasade argues that the evidence of Patrick Ryan
respecting an offer by one Dunphy to sell to Newfoundland and Labrador Housing
Corporation land in the neighbourhood of the expropriated lands for a price of
$1 per square foot was hearsay and inadmissible. In fact, Mr. Ryan learned of
the “offer” from another employee of Newfoundland and Labrador Housing
Corporation and at no time did he discuss the matter with Mr. Dunphy. In the
alternative, the appellant argues that, if admissible, the evidence should not
have been given any weight, especially since the “offer” had not been used by
any of the expert appraisers in forming their opinions.

[
15
]

The respondent, in reply, argues that where
hearsay evidence is the only evidence on a point then the trier of fact may
accept such evidence and deal with its weight in light of all the other factors
which would affect it (
Teperman
&
Sons Ltd. v. Toronto (City
)

(1976), 12 L.C.R. 84 at 90)
and that in this case because of the lack of
pre-hearing disclosure by the appellant the board was left to the less
stringent approach outlined by Mr. Justice Grant in
Billy Club v. Dartmouth
(City)
(1984),
1984 CanLII 5631 (NS SC)
, 62 N.S.R.(2d) 30;
136 A.P.R. 30
;
30 L.C.R. 33 (T.D.)
.

[
16
]

With respect, I do not see that Mr. Justice
Grant was advocating a less stringent approach. He stated that hearsay evidence
may be used by an expert in forming an opinion.

“It is generally considered to be of an
aid to the trier of fact in technical and scientific matters. An expert
generally may rely on his learning during his formal training, his continuing
education, he may refer to texts, periodicals, discussions with others in his
field. He is not restricted to opinions based solely on his own personal
experiences and observations. This by necessity may involve hearsay, (p. 45-46)”

In the
Billy Club

case, Mr. Justice Grant
found the person qualified as an expert was entitled to give hearsay evidence
but hearsay evidence given by an individual who was not an expert was
inadmissible.

[
17
]

In
Teperman v. Municipality of Metropolitan
Toronto
(supra), the Ontario Land Compensation
Board considered a situation where there was unsatisfactory evidence on both
sides - on the one side completely hearsay. Using the
Statutory Powers
Procedures Act
,

1971, they admitted the hearsay but indicated they
would not have done so had the claimant been represented by counsel. We have
not been referred to a similar provision in Newfoundland legislation.

[
18
]

Mr. Ryan’s evidence regarding the Dunphy offer
was by way of background to a description of a study done by Newfoundland and
Labrador Housing Corporation regarding the possibility of developing two of the
parcels of expropriated land (then owned by Newfoundland and Labrador Housing
Corporation) in conjunction with the Dunphy land. The analysis performed by Mr.
Ryan in 1989 was in the context of the “offer”, not in the context of a claim
for compensation. He concluded that at the price of $1 per square foot ($10.77
per square meter) the development would be uneconomic. There is direct evidence
from Charles Harris, another employee of Newfoundland and Labrador Housing Corporation,
that an offer was received though he, an expert witness, did not say what the
price was.

[
19
]

On page 48 of the decision, the board clearly
accepts the offer as having been proven. On page 49, the board states:

“The reality is that the Dunphy land, as
well as Parcels A & B, did not sell in the normal market situation.”

Counsel for the appellant points to this
statement as a clear error on the part of the board. Of course, the Dunphy land
was not sold but in the context of the decision I do not interpret the above
noted statement as a declaration that there had been a sale. Rather, it is an
acknowledgement (albeit perhaps not clearly stated) that those comparables are
not the customary market sales. Indeed, on page 40 of the Award, there is a
statement by the board that the Dunphy land was not sold.

[
20
]

The “Dunphy offer” was used by the board to
indicate an upper limit to the value of Parcels A, 1, 2, 9 and 10.

[
21
]

I agree with the argument of the appellant that
the evidence of Mr. Ryan, to the extent that it is presented for the purpose of
proving the amount of the sale price offered, is inadmissible. On the other
hand, the evidence respecting the analysis performed and the conclusions drawn
regarding the economics of development is clearly admissible.

[
22
]

It is not sufficient, however, to establish that
some evidence was improperly admitted. The appellant must also show that the
wrongly admitted evidence affected the amount awarded. In this case, there was
direct evidence of the existence of the offer and strong circumstantial
evidence of the price. The results of the research done by Newfoundland and
Labrador Housing Corporation would indicate that the acquisition of the Dunphy
lands at $1 per square foot would be uneconomic and for that reason the offer
was not accepted. The economics of a purchase at $1 per square foot and, on
that basis, the decision of Newfoundland and Labrador Housing Corporation not
to purchase the Dunphy land dictated to the board that the upper limit of the
expropriated property was $1 per square foot. In those circumstances, while the
particular piece of evidence may not have been admissible, there was other
stronger evidence to support the conclusion and therefore the appellant has not
established that the admission of that piece of evidence in itself affected the
amount of the award.

[
23
]

This ground of appeal must fail.

Calculation
Of Compensation

[
24
]

Section 27 specifies rules to be used by a board
in fixing the amount of compensation payable for expropriated lands.
Subsections (a) and (b) state:

“27(a) the compensation shall be an
amount based on the fair market value of the land and on existing use value at
the time of the beginning of expropriation proceedings and no account shall be
taken of the compulsory acquisition of the land, the disturbance of the owner
occupier, or other detrimental effect;

“27(b) the fair market value of the land
shall be taken to be the amount that the land, if sold in the open market by a
willing seller, might be expected to realize but the board is entitled to
consider all returns and assessments of capital value for taxation made or
acquiesced in by the owner of the land;”

[
25
]

The appraisers who gave evidence agreed on the
definition of market value. That is, the highest price (sometimes expressed as
the most probable selling price) estimated in terms of money that a property
will bring if exposed for sale on the open market, allowing a reasonable time
to find a purchaser who buys with knowledge of all the uses to which it is
adapted and for which it is capable of being used.

[
26
]

In
Miller et al. v. Newfoundland
,

supra,
this court impliedly recognized that in determining compensation in accordance
with s. 27 there is an assessment of highest and best use. The concept of
highest and best use recognizes that market value may reflect a higher and
better use than the current one. The
Miller
case also recognized that
highest and best use, while acknowledging potential, did not assume the
potential was already realized.

“… the land should therefore be valued
for what it was at the date of taking, namely, a tract of land capable … of
subdivision into lots and of being sold over time. These future advantages,
however, should only be taken into account in so far as they may be regarded as
giving the property its present value.” (p. 330 L.C.R.)

[
27
]

Highest and best use is assessed on the basis of
what is a reasonable expectation at the time of expropriation. Speculative or
unrealistic expectations cannot be used to ground the compensation on a use
which is higher than the current use.

[
28
]

Farlinger Developments Ltd. v. East York
(Borough)
(1975),
1975 CanLII 587 (ON CA)
, 8 L.C.R. 112; 9 O.R.(2d) 553; 61
D.L.R.(3d) 193 (S.C.C.), examined this concept in the context of zoning. At p.
123, Howland, J.A., said:

“From these authorities it would seem to
be established that the highest and best use must be based on something more
than a possibility of rezoning. There must be a probability or a reasonable
expectation that such rezoning will take place. It is not enough that the lands
have the capability of rezoning. In my opinion, probability connotes something
higher than a 50% possibility.”

[
29
]

Lincoln W. North, in his article
The Concept
of Highest and Best Use
,

published under the auspices of the
Research and Development Fund of the Appraisal Institute of Canada, when
considering the question of an alternative use as a basis of highest and best
use, stated at p. 3:

“In other words, for an alternative use
to be considered as a higher and better use than an existing use, there must at
least be a reasonable probability that such (alternative) use will meet all of
the criteria governing its determination. It must not only be reasonably
probable that such alternative use will come into being, either immediately or
in the foreseeable future, but that such higher and better use will be strong enough
to affect the present market value of the property. Otherwise the alternative
use should not be considered as a higher and better use. Stated conversely, it
may be said that a prospective purchaser will seldom pay a premium price for a
property, over and above its value in current use, unless a higher and better
use has a reasonable certainty of being realized. It may therefore be concluded
that circumstances affecting value which depend on events or occurrences which,
while within the realm of possibility, are not expected to be reasonably
probable, should be excluded from consideration in the process of estimating
highest and best use.”

“Market value can therefore be defined as
being the present worth of probable future events.” (Lincoln W. North, supra)

The
Freeze

[
30
]

In September of 1984, the Corner Brook City
Council, after public hearings, imposed a “freeze” on the development of lands
in the area of the proposed new route for the Trans Canada Highway. However,
the zoning applicable to the expropriated lands did not change in 1984 nor
after that date to the time of expropriation. The expropriated lands, which
were within the area of the proposed highway development, were acquired by the
appellant after the “freeze” was imposed.

[
31
]

Lasade submits that the law requires the freeze,
which was imposed at the request of the expropriating authority, be ignored
when arriving at the market value of the expropriated lands at the time of
expropriation. In an interesting juxtaposition, the appellant also argues that
the sales of these same lands to Lasade shortly before the expropriation are
not valid comparable sales because of the existence of the same freeze.

[
32
]

In support of its position, the appellant cites,
in particular,
Halliday’s
Estate
v. Newfoundland Light and Power Co.
(1980),
29 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 212
;
82 A.P.R. 212
;
20 L.C.R. 325 (Nfld. C.A.)
. In the
Halliday

case, this court adopted the view that when an authority either alone or in
concert with another causes an artificial depreciation of the value of the
property it cannot then take advantage of that fact to deprive the owner of the
value of the lands based on the potential development prior to the authority
interfering.

[
33
]

The respondent argues that the appellant’s
knowledge of the restrictions before purchase distinguishes this case from the
Halliday

case. Citing
Kramer et al. v. Wascana Centre Authority
,

1967 CanLII 115 (SCC)
, [1967]
S.C.R. 237 and
Atlantic Shopping Centres Ltd. v. St. John’s
, supra, the
respondent submits that the zoning regime, including the freeze, is relevant to
the determination of land value and must be considered.

[
34
]

The distinction between the
Kramer
and
Atlantic
Shopping Centres
cases, and the
Halliday
case is whether there is a
causal connection between the imposition of the restriction and the
expropriation which ultimately occurs (
R. v. Jewish Community Centre of
Edmonton Trust
(1983), 27 L.C.R. 333 (Alta.) at 360)
. In the
Atlantic
Shopping Centres
case, the
Halliday
case was distinguished because
the expropriated land was subject to the same restrictions and regulations as
all other land in the City of St. John’s.

[
35
]

There is strength in the respondent’s position
that the appellant is in a different position than the owner in the
Halliday

case. Unlike the owner in the
Halliday
case, the appellant was not
the owner when the restrictions on use were imposed; unlike the
Halliday
case,
the appellant purchased knowing that the freeze was in effect and therefore
development was unlikely; unlike the
Halliday
situation, the authority
had done nothing after the property was acquired by the appellant to diminish
market value.

[
36
]

However, the situation is akin to that in the
Halliday

case in a critical way. The freeze was imposed as part of a scheme to use
the land for a particular purpose. The
Halliday
case is a reflection of
the view that, in the absence of a clear legislative directive to that effect,
expropriating authorities will not be permitted to take advantage of
restrictions imposed for reasons related to the expropriation to obtain a
better price than would otherwise apply. For that reason, in this case
compensation must be determined without reference to the freeze.

[
37
]

None of the experts who gave evidence took into
account the existence of the freeze in arriving at an opinion. Moreover, it
must be noted that the board’s rejection of the opinions of all of the experts
but one respecting the highest and best use of the expropriated lands was not
based on the existence of the freeze.

[
38
]

Here, as will be examined, the board concluded
that there was no immediate demand and therefore, with the exception of two
parcels, the highest and best use was to hold for future development. In
determining market value on the basis of it being held for future development,
the board assumes that at some point in the future the lands would be available
for development though not in the short term.

[
39
]

The respondent, in cross-appeal, argues that the
board did not give sufficient weight to the purchase price paid by Lasade or
its shareholder in acquiring the expropriated lands in the first instance. It is
submitted by Lasade that no weight should have been given to this evidence
because, among other factors, when the lands were purchased they were subject
to a freeze.

[
40
]

In
Aldo Recreational Park Ltd. v.
Metropolitan Toronto & Region Conservation Authority
(1975), 9 L.C.R.
102 (Ont. C.A.)
, the Ontario Court of Appeal held that the price the owner had
paid for the property was an appropriate starting point in the enquiry into
market value. One might qualify that statement with the proviso that the
purchase should not have been too remote in time. In this case, time was not a
major concern as the purchases were in 1989 and 1990 and the expropriation was
in 1991. Further, the board held that the market value for vacant land in the
Corner Brook area had been rising prior to 1989 but had been stable from 1989
to the date of expropriation. There is conflicting evidence on this point, as
the board acknowledged, but there is ample evidence to support the board’s
finding.

[
41
]

Like comparable sales of other properties, the price
paid by the owner must be examined to determine if there are factors which
lessen its utility in determining the current market value. Lasade argued that
the existence of the freeze at the time of the purchases by Lasade made this
information irrelevant to the task at hand which was to determine value without
reference to the freeze. The implication of this argument is that the freeze
influenced the price to Lasade’s benefit. In fact, the board found that there
was no evidence of any actual losses of sales or actual diminution of values
because of the freeze. The board held that despite some qualifications, the
purchase prices, in fact, were more reliable comparables than many of the
comparable sales chosen by the appraisers. In doing so, the board noted that
these purchases had been made from four different sellers; an individual, two
corporations and a Crown agency. It was also the board’s conclusion that the
expropriated lands had not been acquired by Lasade at inordinately low prices.

[
42
]

In the context of the market place, what the
original owner sold to Lasade was land which probably would be expropriated or,
alternatively, released for development in the future. In either event,
compensation would be based on potential not hampered by the freeze. So then
the purchase price, as the board held, becomes a very important indicator of
value.

Application
Of Principles Of Valuation

[
43
]

Lasade argues that the board made numerous
errors in the method used and in the conclusions drawn. Generally, these
submissions can be summarized in the arguments that the board was in error
where it chose to accept the reasoning or conclusion of the appraiser Gordon
Brewer and reject or fail to consider the evidence, opinions or conclusions of
the appraisers Marc Andrews, Gordon Nagle and Ed Allen. The appellant alleges
that Mr. Brewer did not use proper principles in selecting comparable sales and
making adjustments in his analysis of the sales and as a result the board was
in error to the extent that it relied on his evidence.

[
44
]

It must be remembered that a board is not
obliged to accept the evidence of the experts. It can make its own judgment (
La-Coste
v. Cedar Rapids Manufacturing & Power Co.
,

1928 CanLII 348 (UK JCPC)
, [1928] 2 D.L.R. 1
(P.C);
Marcus v. Canada National Capital Commission
,
1969 CanLII 44 (SCC)
, [1970] S.C.R. 39; 8
D.L.R.(3d) 671. In
Westphal Estates Ltd., Re
(1976),
1976 CanLII 2527 (NS CA)
, 17 N.S.R.(2d) 273;

19 A.P.R. 273
;
10 L.C.R. 289 (C.A.) at 291 [L.C.R.]
, MacKeigan, C.J.N.S.,
expressed it as follows:

‘‘To determine value the ‘widely
different views’ … must be examined to find out the reasons for the
differences. In doing so, some of the data used by them to support their views
may have to be discarded as not sufficiently probative, such as sales of lands
which, because of variance in time of sale, in serviceability of the land, or in
the location or type of land, cannot be considered as true or appropriate ‘comparables’.
All relevant data and other evidence presented by all expert witnesses, … must
then be considered by the Judge so as to determine on a reasoned basis what in
his opinion is the value of the land as of November 10, 1971. He may decide to
adopt, as being closest to the probable ‘right’ value, the value placed on the
land by a particular appraiser, or he may derive from his logical analysis some
value differing from that suggested by an expert. The task of determining
compensation cannot, I respectfully suggest, be carried out by merely choosing
between experts’ valuations on the preferences of other witnesses.”

[
45
]

In this case, the board noted several reasons,
all in my view valid, for arriving at an independent assessment.

[
46
]

On page 39 of the award the board states:

“The evidence of the expert witnesses was
reflected in extensive written reports; unfortunately, these reports contained
much superficial information and not much substantial analysis. Conclusions
seem to have been arrived at with surprising ease and subjectivity. There was
such a diversity of conclusions drawn by the expert witnesses, that, to some
degree, the evidence is distrusted. In some cases the values arrived at by Mr.
Andrews are almost ten times the values presented by Mr. Brewer. Appraised
values appearing in reports prepared for the claimant are generally about five
or six times the values of Mr. Brewer. In the case of Parcels 9 and 10, Mr.
Andrews’ value is 41% higher than that of Mr. Nagle.

“There is considerable question with
respect to the reliability of comparables variously employed. There is a lack
of consistency in what the appraisers viewed as being usable comparables sales.
This diversity of comparables likely explains the wide range of appraised
values.”

[
47
]

These paragraphs reflect the understandable
doubt raised in the minds of the arbitrators faced with experts who, using
ostensibly the same method and with knowledge of the same comparable sales,
arrive at such divergent opinions. The appellant has not established that the
board was in error in these observations and conclusions.

[
48
]

In the award, the board was critical of all of
the appraiser witnesses who they found unabashedly supported the position of
the party who called them. An appraiser, like any expert witness, should be
fully prepared. This generally requires some exchange of information and
cooperation with counsel for the party calling the appraiser. However, this
should not be allowed to interfere with the expert’s opinion. In the text
Expropriation
in Canada
by Kenneth J. Boyd, at p. 139 the author summarizes the position
as follows:

“The expert owes to the client who
engages him a duty to assess the problem at hand in the most favourable light
which the facts and circumstances will reasonably permit. However, the
fulfilment of that duty must not be allowed to overshadow the primary
obligation of the expert which is to provide an assessment and opinion arrived
at on an independent and professional basis.”

In the case of Mr. Andrews, there was ample
evidence to support the conclusion that he was not independent. Most notable
was the acknowledged reliance by Mr. Andrews on counsel for the appellant (who
is also the principal shareholder of Lasade) for guidance on the principles to
be applied. Mr. Andrews held no formal accreditation but was declared to be an
expert on the basis of his work experience.

[
49
]

The board agreed with the appraisers and the
appellant that the market data approach was the most appropriate but quite
properly qualified this by noting that suitable market data must be available.
The board opined that the appraisers in this case should have been more
discriminating in their selection of market data. The board then stated that where
an adjustment of 50% is necessary the data is considered to be insufficiently
comparable to be reliable. It is hard to fault the board for this conclusion.
The greater the differences in the comparable sales and the subject the greater
the number of adjustments which must be made. The greater the number of
adjustments the more subjective elements enter the equation and the less
reliable the data. There is no doubt a point where the comparable would have so
little value as to be quite properly disregarded by a board. I find no error in
the board’s conclusion that when the adjustments amount to 50% they are not
sufficiently alike to be used as comparables.

[
50
]

In performing its own assessment of highest and
best use based on the evidence which had been presented, the board chose four
of the nine factors listed by Lincoln W. North in the article
The Concept of
Highest and Best Use
as being relevant in this case. The four chosen were:
profitability, physical and functional limitations, marketability, and titular restrictions.
The appellant acknowledges that the circumstances of the particular piece of
property dictate which factors are applicable. The factors chosen by the board
were appropriate ones.

[
51
]

In examining the factor of profitability, the
board noted Lasade had not presented evidence on development costs. The board
did not, as the appellant submitted, suggest that this type of evidence was
essential but rather expressed surprise at this gap in relevant evidence in the
claimant’s case. The only evidence respecting profitability was presented by
the respondent in respect of Parcels 9 and 10 and Parcels A and B (B was not
expropriated but evidence respecting its value was considered by the board to
be relevant, as indeed it was). The factor of profitability is of importance
because where the highest and best use is not economically feasible a board is
justified in rejecting that use for the purpose of valuing the property (
Guido
v. Canada (Ministry of Transportation & Communications
)
(1977),
13 L.C.R. 97 (Ont. C.A.), at 98)
. As the board noted, “a prudent purchaser
would undertake some sort of cost/benefit analysis before reaching a conclusion
with respect to the market value of a parcel of land” (p. 44 of Award). This is
particularly true if the land was being purchased for commercial or industrial
purposes.

[
52
]

The board noted that the terrain and slope
affected market value. The board believed that certain cost items would be
addressed by potential customers: the need for excavation; installation of
services, especially water at higher elevations; upgrading of existing
services; and construction of internal access roads. There was evidence that in
respect of some or all of the expropriated lands these factors were relevant
and therefore the board was correct in taking them into consideration.
Obviously, there is a relationship between these potential costs and
profitability. There was a great deal of testimony as to whether the
expropriated lands were serviced or not. The evidence was clear that there were
services near the lands. However, it was equally clear that if, as was
contended, for highest and best use the properties were to be developed by
subdividing, this would involve extending services and added costs to the
developer. The factor was addressed in oral evidence but was not adequately
addressed in the reports prepared by the experts as a consideration in arriving
at their opinions on market value.

[
53
]

As to marketability, the board found that the
appraisers had not taken into account all of the relevant factors and that
there was no cogent evidence of any expectation of development of much of the
expropriated land within a reasonable period of time. Lasade submits that the
doubts expressed by the board regarding the economy of the City of Corner Brook
are in error, as are the board’s findings: that there is not a need for land
suitable and capable for commercial use and development; that the need fpr
industrial building lots has been greatly satisfied; and there is no
foreseeable substantial increase in demand. In particular, Lasade points to the
fact that certain businesses already established have expanded and others have
relocated to the Maple Valley Road area.

[
54
]

In contrast to this, the board chose to
emphasize the evidence of the history of the expropriated lands. In particular,
it was pointed out that Parcels A and B, which were part of the lands
accumulated by Newfoundland and Labrador Housing Corporation for the Maple
Valley Road Industrial Park, had been available for development for 20 years
and no one other than the appellant, who purchased for speculation, had shown
any interest in the lands. Further, the unex-propriated portion of Parcel B,
which was already zoned general industrial and no longer encumbered by the
freeze, was still undeveloped in 1991 and there was no evidence that there were
plans to do so. Only Parcels 9 and 10 were found to have an expectation of
development within a reasonable time. All of the experts who expressed opinions
on the subject agreed respecting the highest and best use for Parcels 9 and 10.
Here the board weighed the evidence presented and having done so made a finding
of fact which though contrary to the opinions of some was supportable on the
evidence presented.

[
55
]

Under the heading Titular Restrictions, the
board was concerned primarily with the existence of Crown rights-of-way through
the expropriated lands, both on the issue of satisfactory access to the
properties and with the need to obtain the cooperation of the respondent to
obtain title to the rights-of-way to facilitate development. In respect of
Parcels 1 and 2, the respondent argues these lots were under disabilities
because access was only via a 20 foot right-of-way. However, the appellant
believes that this last disability was overcome when Lasade acquired Parcels 1
and 2 as it had already owned the neighbouring property (Parcels A and B)
thereby allowing for the possibility of alternate access. The board also noted
the difficulties with access to Larch Street for two of the lots. These factors
were not viewed as major obstacles by the board but they were seen as adding to
the time delay before any development of the expropriated lands might be
reasonable.

[
56
]

The appellant argues that the board was in error
in rejecting the evidence of Denis Knight, an expert in land use planning,
respecting the probability of rezoning and the highest and best use. It has
been suggested that planners should give the evidence on highest and best use
and appraisers should be used to give evidence respecting compensation.
However, appraisers have a high degree of expertise in assessing the potential
of a property for development and as a matter of practice regularly give
evidence as to the suitability of property for re-zoning as part of their
assessment of highest and best use, though it might be wise to establish the
experience of the witness in this area when he or she is being qualified.

[
57
]

As has already been noted, if highest and best
use would require a zoning change it must be based on a probability or a
reasonable expectation that the rezoning will take place. The appellant
concedes that the onus is on the claimant to establish that there was a
reasonable expectation or a clear probability that the zoning claimed would be
granted. Further, he seems to concede that he must establish that rezoning was
possible as of the date of expropriation. The impact of the freeze on zoning
has already been examined. The board did not reject the view that rezoning
would be possible. Rather, the board found that there was not the demand for
the property and that in the current market, factors such as physical
conditions would operate against the use of the property for the purpose
suggested.

[
58
]

In arriving at its own value respecting the
expropriated lands, the board held that two purchases by the Provincial Government
were not good comparables because “in addition to location and other factors,
its ‘special buyer’ status as a purchaser puts the respondent in a vulnerable
position in the open market”. One assumes “location” refers to the fact that
the lands were adjacent to the Trans Canada Highway and “other factors” include
zoning as Highway Tourist Commercial. The appellant argues that in this the
board was in error as there had been an agreed statement of facts which
acknowledged that these purchases were after free and willing negotiations and
therefore the historic reason for ignoring such sales was not present.
Certainly, the evidence would have permitted the board to conclude that in
respect of bargaining position this was a valid comparison. However, the
location and other factors make it a less valuable comparable than those chosen
by the board.

[
59
]

Lasade cites a number of cases which reject
municipal assessments as a basis for valuation and implies that the board was
in error by basing valuation on municipal assessments. However, the board made
only an observation that its opinions were more consistent with the municipal
assessments than with the appraisers conclusions. There is no statement that
municipal assessments entered into the board’s calculations. Similarly, the
board’s comment that the lands were acquired for speculative purposes was not a
factor in calculating compensation.

[
60
]

Lasade also makes submissions regarding the
credibility of certain witnesses. Credibility is a matter for the board.

Interest

[
61
]

Sections 35 and 36 of the
Act
specify the
rate of interest and from when it is to run. Those sections state:

“35. The Minister shall pay the
compensation awarded by a board within six months after the date on which the
award was made, and, where the compensation is not paid within 30 days after
the date on which the award was made, it shall after the end of 30 days bear
interest at the rate of 5% a year until it is paid.

“36. Notwithstanding section 35, a board
may, at the time of awarding compensation, direct that interest

(a) at the
rate referred to in that section; and

(b) covering
part or all of the period between the date of the vesting of title under this
Act and the date that the compensation starts to bear interest under section 35

shall be paid to the person to whom the
compensation is awarded, after consideration has been given by the board to
action or inaction on the part of

(c) the person
to whom the compensation is awarded;

(d) the
representatives of the person to whom the compensation is awarded; and

(e) the
minister.

and the minister shall pay the interest
directed to be paid.”

[
62
]

Clearly, the board had the authority under the
Act

to award interest at the rate of 5% a year from 30 days after the date of
the award and for part or all of the period from the date of vesting to the
date that compensation starts to bear interest under s. 35. In its order, the
board merely stated that the appellant was entitled to interest as set out in
the
Expropriation Act.
Counsel for the respondent concedes the appellant
is entitled to interest from the date of vesting. The board not having
specified the date of commencement, the award will be amended to state that
interest is to commence from the date of vesting and run to the date of payment
at the rate of 5% per year.

Costs

[
63
]

The appellant seeks an order for costs on a
solicitor-client basis from the date of expropriation. Section 34, which
enables the board to award costs, also determines on what basis the costs are
to be taxed. The appellant is entitled to that specified in the section. I
agree with the argument of the respondent that s. 48 has no application in this
case. Section 48 which allows the court to order costs between solicitor and
client is limited to those cases in which there has been a petition before a
judge of the Trial Division. The award of costs by the board shall be as
specified by s. 34 of the
Act.

Summary

[
64
]

It has not been established that the board
proceeded on a wrong principle or so misapprehended the evidence that the award
is excessive or inadequate. In particular, the board was not in error in
rejecting the hearsay evidence respecting motivation. While it was in error in
admitting the hearsay evidence of the amount of the offer, that error was not
shown to have materially effected the conclusion. In respect of the freeze, the
board did not take it into account in holding that immediate commercial
development was not probable. Rather, other factors were clearly influential in
the board’s conclusion. The board, as it was entitled to do, using the evidence
presented to it and accepted methods of valuation arrived at its own value for
the expropriated lands. It has not been shown to be in error in doing so.

[
65
]

The appeal and the cross-appeal must fail. The
parties shall bear their own costs on this appeal.

Appeal dismissed;

cross-appeal dismissed.
